explanations.answer: Moses already gave them land east of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "For Moses had given the inheritance east of the Jordan to the other two and a half tribes." Their slice was already off the tray before the lot-drawing started. Nobody was left out of the line, they had just been served early.

explanations.answer: They will get the land left over at the end
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think that, friend. Nothing in the text says anything about leftovers. It says Moses had already given them their inheritance east of the Jordan (Joshua 14:3). Their land was settled, so the lot only had to cover the other nine and a half tribes.

explanations.answer: They have to win their land in battle first
explanations.explanation: Close, but no battle is mentioned here. Joshua 14:3 says Moses had already given the two and a half tribes their inheritance east of the Jordan. Their plate was full before this meal began, so they weren't waiting on a fight. They were already home.

Cities it is. The text says no portion of the land went to the Levites, "except for cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds." So the Levites had places to live and room for their animals. Not a bad deal, baker.

Tents sound right, friend, because Israel lived in them in the wilderness. But this verse says the Levites got "cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds." That's a real address, with room for the animals. The tent days were behind them.

Caves, huh? I admit I've lived somewhere with no windows and a lot of dust, so I get the pull. But Joshua 14:4 says the Levites got cities to live in, plus pasturelands for their flocks and herds. No caves on the list, baker.

explanations.answer: He remained loyal to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Caleb says, "I remained loyal to the LORD my God." His brothers who went with him made the hearts of the people melt with fear, and he did not go that way. The same trip, two very different reports.

explanations.answer: He stayed quiet in the camp
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Caleb doesn't say he kept quiet. He says he brought back "an honest report" and "remained loyal to the LORD my God" (Joshua 14:7-8). A man who stays quiet doesn't talk about his report forty-five years later like it's framed on the wall.

explanations.answer: He went back to spy again
explanations.explanation: A second spy trip would be a lot of walking, baker. But Caleb never says that. He says he brought back an honest report, and while his brothers made the people's hearts melt with fear, he "remained loyal to the LORD my God" (Joshua 14:7-8). One trip, one honest report.

explanations.answer: The land his feet had walked on
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses swore, "Surely the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever." Caleb's footprints were the claim. I'd say walking that far to get a promise is a decent way to earn one, friend.

The Jordan is the wrong river for this one, baker. Moses swore that "the land on which you have set foot" would be Caleb's inheritance (Joshua 14:9). That land was where Caleb had walked as a spy. The land east of the Jordan was a different matter, given to the other two and a half tribes (Joshua 14:3).

Gilgal is where Caleb is standing while he talks, friend, but it's not what Moses promised him. Moses swore, "Surely the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever." The promise was about the ground Caleb had walked as a spy, not the ground under his sandals at that moment.
Eighty-five, and Caleb says so himself: "here I am today, eighty-five years old." Forty plus forty-five does it. Math works even when the oven's on, baker.

So close, friend. Forty plus forty-five lands on eighty-five, and Caleb says it himself: "here I am today, eighty-five years old" (Joshua 14:10). You were five years short. I once lost count of how long I sat in a drawer, so no judgment here.

Ninety is five too many, baker. Forty plus forty-five is eighty-five, and Caleb says it himself: "here I am today, eighty-five years old" (Joshua 14:10). He's got plenty of years already without anyone adding extra.

True. Caleb says he's "still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out." Then he adds, "As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in." Eighty-five and ready to go, baker. I'm over here stretching just to reach the top shelf.

It's actually true, friend. Caleb says he's "still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out." He goes on, "As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in" (Joshua 14:11). He doesn't say he's slowed down at all.

Right, baker. Caleb says, "Perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken." He knew about the fortified cities and still pointed to the LORD's help. His plan started with the LORD, not with his own muscles.

Joshua is standing right there, so I see why you'd think so. But Caleb never mentions an army. He says, "Perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken" (Joshua 14:12). The help he names is the LORD's.

A siege would be a very patient plan, friend. But Caleb doesn't mention one. He says, "Perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken" (Joshua 14:12). The only help he names is the LORD's.
Not true, baker. Joshua doesn't turn Caleb down. The text says, "Then Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance." Caleb asked and Caleb got a blessing with it.
False is right. Joshua doesn't send Caleb away. "Then Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance." He got the blessing and the land, friend.

Anakim is right. The text says Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, "after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim." Those are the same Anakim Caleb mentioned earlier, with their great and fortified cities (Joshua 14:12). Fancy name, baker, but Hebron suits it better.

Amorites are a real people in the Bible, friend, but they aren't who this verse names. It says Kiriath-arba was named "after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim" (Joshua 14:15). The Anakim are the ones Caleb mentioned just a few verses earlier.

The Philistines are a real people in the Bible, baker, but the verse doesn't name them here. It says Kiriath-arba was named "after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim" (Joshua 14:15). Same Anakim Caleb warned Joshua about, with the fortified cities.
